prompt: Backstage is described as a framework for building Internal Developer Portals (IDPs). Which three core features ship with the open-source project out of the box?
options: Software Catalog, Software Templates, and TechDocs
CI/CD pipelines, a container registry, and a secrets manager
A Kubernetes distribution, a service mesh, and an ingress controller
An issue tracker, a wiki, and a chat client
optionNotes: Correct. The Software Catalog (ownership and metadata), Software Templates via the Scaffolder (golden paths), and TechDocs (docs-like-code) are the three core features bundled with Backstage, extended by a plugin ecosystem.
Backstage integrates with CI/CD, registries, and secret stores through plugins, but it does not ship or run these systems itself.
Backstage is a Node.js/React web application, not a Kubernetes distribution or networking layer; the Kubernetes plugin only visualises workloads.
Backstage surfaces links to issue trackers and chat tools through entity annotations, but it does not replace them.
explanation: Backstage is an open platform (a CNCF project originally built by Spotify) for building developer portals. Its three core features are the Software Catalog, Software Templates (Scaffolder), and TechDocs; everything else comes from the plugin ecosystem. It is not itself a CI system, cluster, or ticketing tool.
example:
# create a new Backstage app (interactive prompts for name)
npx @backstage/create-app@latest
cd my-portal
yarn start   # runs frontend + backend in dev mode
# http://localhost:3000 -> Catalog, Create (templates), Docs (TechDocs)
diagram:
flowchart TD
    IDP["Backstage developer portal"]
    IDP --> C["Software Catalog"]
    IDP --> T["Software Templates / Scaffolder"]
    IDP --> D["TechDocs"]
    IDP --> P["Plugin ecosystem"]
    P --> K["Kubernetes, CI, Search, etc"]

prompt: In a `catalog-info.yaml` describing a `kind: Component` entity, which two `spec` fields are required by the catalog's validation?
options: `spec.type` and `spec.owner`
`spec.lifecycle` and `spec.system`
`spec.owner` and `spec.dependsOn`
`spec.type` and `spec.providesApis`
optionNotes: Correct. A Component must declare `spec.type` (for example `service`, `website`, `library`), `spec.owner` (an entity ref such as `group:default/team-a`), and `spec.lifecycle`; `type` and `owner` are the two listed here that are mandatory.
`spec.lifecycle` is indeed required, but `spec.system` is optional and only creates a `partOf` relation when present.
`spec.owner` is required, but `spec.dependsOn` is an optional list of entity refs.
`spec.type` is required, but `spec.providesApis` is optional and only relevant when the component exposes APIs.
explanation: The Component kind requires `spec.type`, `spec.lifecycle`, and `spec.owner`; the catalog rejects entities missing them. Fields like `system`, `dependsOn`, `providesApis`, and `consumesApis` are optional and exist to generate relations to other entities.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    github.com/project-slug: acme/payments-api
spec:
  type: service       # required
  lifecycle: production # required
  owner: group:default/payments-team  # required
  system: checkout    # optional -> partOf relation
diagram:
flowchart LR
    F["catalog-info.yaml"] --> K["kind: Component"]
    K --> T["spec.type required"]
    K --> L["spec.lifecycle required"]
    K --> O["spec.owner required"]
    K --> S["spec.system optional"]
    O -->|"ownedBy"| G["Group entity"]

prompt: Which of these are well-known relation types that the Backstage catalog generates between entities? (Select all that apply.)
options: `ownedBy` / `ownerOf`
`dependsOn` / `dependencyOf`
`partOf` / `hasPart`
`deployedTo` / `hostOf`
`linkedWith` / `linkedBy`
optionNotes: Correct. `spec.owner` on a Component, API, Resource, System, or Domain produces an `ownedBy` relation, and the reverse `ownerOf` on the Group or User.
Correct. `spec.dependsOn` on Components and Resources yields `dependsOn`, with `dependencyOf` on the target.
Correct. `spec.system` on a Component/API/Resource, `spec.domain` on a System, and `spec.subcomponentOf` all produce `partOf`, with `hasPart` on the parent.
There is no built-in `deployedTo` relation; deployment targets are surfaced by plugins such as Kubernetes using annotations, not catalog relations.
`linkedWith` is not a catalog relation. Links to external URLs live in `metadata.links` and do not create relations.
explanation: The catalog derives relations from spec fields: `ownedBy`/`ownerOf` from `spec.owner`, `dependsOn`/`dependencyOf` from `spec.dependsOn`, `partOf`/`hasPart` from `spec.system`, `spec.domain`, and `spec.subcomponentOf`, plus `providesApi`/`apiProvidedBy`, `consumesApi`/`apiConsumedBy`, and `memberOf`/`hasMember`. `deployedTo` and `linkedWith` are not part of the well-known relation set.
example:
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: orders-service
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: team-orders           # -> ownedBy group:default/team-orders
  system: checkout             # -> partOf system:default/checkout
  dependsOn:
    - resource:default/orders-db  # -> dependsOn
  providesApis:
    - orders-api                 # -> providesApi
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["Component orders-service"] -->|"ownedBy"| G["Group team-orders"]
    C -->|"partOf"| S["System checkout"]
    C -->|"dependsOn"| R["Resource orders-db"]
    C -->|"providesApi"| A["API orders-api"]
    S -->|"partOf"| D["Domain commerce"]

prompt: In the Backstage catalog backend, what is the difference between an entity provider and a processor?
options: Entity providers are the source of truth that emit entities into the catalog (for example from GitHub or LDAP); processors then validate, enrich, and emit relations for entities during ingestion
Entity providers render entity pages in the frontend; processors run in the backend
Processors are the only way to add entities, while entity providers are deprecated aliases
Entity providers store entities in the database; processors serve the REST API
optionNotes: Correct. Providers own the lifecycle of the entities they inject (full or delta mutations) and are the source of truth; processors run in a pipeline over every entity to validate, transform, emit relations, and emit child entities.
Both providers and processors are backend concepts registered on the catalog plugin; neither has anything to do with React entity pages.
Providers are the modern, preferred way to bulk-ingest entities. Processors can still emit entities (for example from a Location), but they are not the sole mechanism.
Persistence and the REST API are handled by the catalog engine itself, not by providers or processors.
explanation: An `EntityProvider` connects to an external source and tells the catalog exactly which entities exist, using `applyMutation` with `full` or `delta` sets. A `CatalogProcessor` runs on each entity as it flows through the processing pipeline, validating it, emitting relations, or emitting additional entities. Static `catalog.locations` in `app-config.yaml` are fed in through the built-in config-based provider.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    GH["GitHub org"] --> EP["EntityProvider"]
    CFG["app-config catalog.locations"] --> EP2["Config EntityProvider"]
    EP -->|"applyMutation"| Q["Processing pipeline"]
    EP2 --> Q
    Q --> P1["Processor validate"]
    P1 --> P2["Processor emit relations"]
    P2 --> DB["Catalog database"]

prompt: Once a `catalog-info.yaml` has been registered as a Location, the catalog only reads it once; later edits to the file in Git are not picked up unless the entity is deleted and re-registered.
explanation: The catalog continuously refreshes registered locations on a processing interval (by default roughly every 100-150 seconds with jitter, configurable via `catalog.processingInterval`), so changes committed to the file appear automatically. Users can also trigger an immediate refresh via the entity page's refresh button or the `/refresh` API. Deleting and re-registering is never required for ordinary edits.
example:
# app-config.yaml
catalog:
  processingInterval: { minutes: 3 }   # how often locations are re-read
  locations:
    - type: url
      target: https://github.com/acme/payments-api/blob/main/catalog-info.yaml

# force an immediate refresh of one entity
curl -X POST http://localhost:7007/api/catalog/refresh \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"entityRef":"component:default/payments-api"}'
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as "Developer"
    participant Git as "Git repo"
    participant Cat as "Catalog backend"
    Dev->>Git: "commit change to catalog-info.yaml"
    loop "every processingInterval"
        Cat->>Git: "fetch registered Location"
        Git-->>Cat: "updated YAML"
        Cat->>Cat: "reprocess and store entity"
    end

prompt: In a Scaffolder `template.yaml`, what is the `action` id of the built-in step that creates a new GitHub repository and pushes the generated workspace contents to it?
explanation: `publish:github` is the built-in publish action from the GitHub scaffolder module. It takes a `repoUrl` (usually `github.com?owner=...&repo=...`), initialises the repository, pushes the workspace, and outputs `remoteUrl` and `repoContentsUrl` that later steps (such as `catalog:register`) consume. Sibling actions exist for GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure, and Gerrit.
example:
steps:
  - id: fetch
    name: Fetch skeleton
    action: fetch:template
    input:
      url: ./skeleton
      values:
        name: ${{ parameters.name }}
  - id: publish
    name: Publish to GitHub
    action: publish:github
    input:
      repoUrl: ${{ parameters.repoUrl }}   # github.com?owner=acme&repo=my-svc
      defaultBranch: main
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["parameters"] --> F["fetch:template"]
    F -->|"workspace files"| PG["publish:github"]
    PG -->|"remoteUrl, repoContentsUrl"| CR["catalog:register"]
    CR --> CAT["Software Catalog"]

prompt: A software template successfully creates a repository, but the new service never appears in the Software Catalog. Which step is most likely missing from the template?
options: A `catalog:register` step that registers the published `catalog-info.yaml` as a Location
A `fetch:plain` step that downloads the catalog database
A `debug:log` step that prints the entity to the console
A `catalog:fetch` step that reads the new entity
optionNotes: Correct. `catalog:register` takes `repoContentsUrl` (from the publish step) plus `catalogInfoPath`, or a direct `catalogInfoUrl`, and registers that file as a catalog Location so the entity is ingested.
`fetch:plain` copies files into the workspace; it has nothing to do with catalog registration and the database is never downloaded.
`debug:log` is only a diagnostic action that writes messages to the task log.
`catalog:fetch` reads existing entities from the catalog into template context; it does not register new ones.
explanation: Publishing a repository does not tell the catalog about it. The `catalog:register` action creates a Location entity pointing at the repository's `catalog-info.yaml`, after which the catalog processes and displays the Component. The typical template chain is `fetch:template` -> `publish:github` -> `catalog:register`, with an output link to the new entity.
example:
- id: register
    name: Register in catalog
    action: catalog:register
    input:
      repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}
      catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml
output:
  links:
    - title: Open in catalog
      icon: catalog
      entityRef: ${{ steps.register.output.entityRef }}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    PUB["publish:github"] -->|"repoContentsUrl"| REG["catalog:register"]
    REG -->|"creates Location"| LOC["Location entity"]
    LOC -->|"processed"| COMP["Component appears in catalog"]
    REG -->|"entityRef"| OUT["template output link"]

prompt: Which `apiVersion` and `kind` should a current Scaffolder template file declare so that it is accepted by the catalog and the Scaffolder?
options: `apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3` with `kind: Template`
`apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1` with `kind: Template`
`apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1` with `kind: Scaffold`
`apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1` with `kind: Component` and `spec.type: template`
optionNotes: Correct. Templates use `scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3`; this version introduced the `${{ }}` templating syntax, `parameters` (JSON Schema forms), and `steps` that call actions.
`backstage.io/v1alpha1` is the apiVersion for ordinary catalog kinds like Component and System; the Scaffolder rejects Template entities that use it.
There is no `Scaffold` kind and no `v1` scaffolder apiVersion.
A Component with `type: template` is just a regular component; it would not appear on the Create page or be executable by the Scaffolder.
explanation: Software templates are catalog entities of `kind: Template` with `apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3`. The `spec` holds `parameters` (one or more JSON Schema pages rendered as forms), `steps` (action invocations that can reference `${{ parameters.x }}` and `${{ steps.id.output.y }}`), and optional `output`. Earlier `v1beta2` templates used a different templating syntax and are no longer supported.
example:
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: node-service
  title: Node.js service
spec:
  owner: group:default/platform
  type: service
  parameters:
    - title: Basics
      required: [name]
      properties:
        name: { type: string, ui:autofocus: true }
  steps:
    - id: fetch
      action: fetch:template
      input: { url: ./skeleton, values: { name: '${{ parameters.name }}' } }
diagram:
flowchart TD
    T["kind: Template v1beta3"] --> PA["spec.parameters JSON Schema forms"]
    T --> ST["spec.steps action calls"]
    T --> OU["spec.output links"]
    PA -->|"parameters.name"| ST
    ST -->|"steps.id.output"| OU

prompt: Which `metadata.annotations` key must be added to an entity so that TechDocs knows where to find its `mkdocs.yml` and documentation source?
explanation: The `backstage.io/techdocs-ref` annotation points TechDocs at the docs source. `dir:.` means the `mkdocs.yml` sits next to `catalog-info.yaml` in the same repository, `dir:./docs-root` a subdirectory, and `url:https://...` a different location entirely. Without the annotation the Docs tab shows a missing-annotation message.
example:
# catalog-info.yaml
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.   # mkdocs.yml is next to this file

# mkdocs.yml
site_name: Payments API
nav:
  - Home: index.md
plugins:
  - techdocs-core
diagram:
flowchart LR
    E["Entity catalog-info.yaml"] -->|"backstage.io/techdocs-ref dir:."| SRC["mkdocs.yml + docs/"]
    SRC --> B["TechDocs builder mkdocs"]
    B --> HTML["static site"]
    HTML --> UI["Docs tab on entity page"]

prompt: In `app-config.yaml`, a team sets `techdocs.builder: 'external'` and `techdocs.publisher.type: 'awsS3'`. What does this configuration mean for how documentation is produced and served?
options: Docs are built by an external pipeline (for example CI running `techdocs-cli generate` and `publish`) and Backstage only reads the finished sites from the S3 bucket
The Backstage backend runs MkDocs on demand for every request and caches the output in S3
Backstage delegates rendering to an external SaaS documentation service
TechDocs is disabled; the S3 setting is ignored
optionNotes: Correct. The recommended production setup: CI builds docs with `techdocs-cli` and uploads them to object storage; the Backstage backend acts as a read-only server for that storage.
That describes the `local` builder mode, where the backend generates docs itself on first view (and refreshes when the source changes). It is suited to demos and small installs, not production.
There is no SaaS renderer; `external` refers to a build pipeline you own.
TechDocs remains enabled; the publisher configuration is exactly what tells the backend where finished sites live.
explanation: `techdocs.builder` has two values: `local` (the backend generates docs using MkDocs, either natively or via the `techdocs` Docker image) and `external` (some other system generates them). `techdocs.publisher` chooses where the generated sites are stored: `local` filesystem, `awsS3`, `googleGcs`, `azureBlobStorage`, or `openStackSwift`. The recommended production architecture is the external builder with cloud storage.
example:
# app-config.production.yaml
techdocs:
  builder: 'external'   # CI generates the docs
  publisher:
    type: 'awsS3'
    awsS3:
      bucketName: 'acme-techdocs'
      region: 'eu-west-1'

# in CI
npx @techdocs/cli generate --no-docker
npx @techdocs/cli publish --publisher-type awsS3 \
  --storage-name acme-techdocs --entity default/component/payments-api
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CI["CI pipeline"] -->|"techdocs-cli generate"| SITE["HTML site"]
    SITE -->|"techdocs-cli publish"| S3["S3 bucket"]
    S3 -->|"read only"| BE["Backstage TechDocs backend"]
    BE --> FE["Docs tab"]

prompt: Using the new Backstage backend system, a developer wants their plugin to obtain a logger and an HTTP router at startup. Which pattern is correct?
options: Call `createBackendPlugin` with a `register(env)` function that calls `env.registerInit({ deps: { logger: coreServices.logger, httpRouter: coreServices.httpRouter }, async init({ logger, httpRouter }) { ... } })`
Export a `createRouter(env: PluginEnvironment)` function and wire it in `packages/backend/src/plugins/<name>.ts`
Instantiate `new Logger()` and `express.Router()` directly inside the plugin module's top-level code
Declare the services in `app-config.yaml` under `backend.services` and the framework injects them as globals
optionNotes: Correct. In the new backend system, plugins declare service dependencies on `coreServices` (logger, httpRouter, database, config, auth, httpAuth, scheduler, and so on) and the framework resolves and injects them into `init`; the plugin is then added with `backend.add(import('...'))`.
That is the legacy backend pattern with `PluginEnvironment` and per-plugin files, which has been removed in favour of `createBackendPlugin` and `backend.add()`.
Creating services manually bypasses dependency injection, configuration, and shared instrumentation; plugins should not construct core services themselves.
Service wiring is done in code through dependency declarations; there is no `backend.services` config block that injects globals.
explanation: The new backend system centres on `createBackendPlugin` (and `createBackendModule` for extensions). Inside `register`, `registerInit` declares `deps` on service references such as `coreServices.logger` and `coreServices.httpRouter`; the framework instantiates them and calls `init`. The app's `packages/backend/src/index.ts` simply calls `backend.add(import('@internal/plugin-x-backend'))`, replacing the old `PluginEnvironment` plumbing.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    IDX["packages/backend index.ts backend.add"] --> PL["createBackendPlugin pluginId todo"]
    PL --> RI["registerInit deps"]
    RI --> L["coreServices.logger"]
    RI --> H["coreServices.httpRouter"]
    L --> INIT["init receives instances"]
    H --> INIT
    INIT --> API["/api/todo routes"]

prompt: Backstage search gathers documents through collators that run in the backend on a schedule; the default catalog and TechDocs collators are backend modules, and the frontend only queries the resulting index.
explanation: The search backend runs collators (for example `catalog-collator` and `techdocs-collator`) on a scheduler, optionally passes documents through decorators, and writes them to a search engine (Lunr by default, or Postgres, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch). The frontend `SearchPage` and `SearchBar` just call the search API and render results; they do not index anything themselves.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    SCH["Scheduler"] --> CC["Catalog collator"]
    SCH --> TC["TechDocs collator"]
    CC --> DEC["Decorators optional"]
    TC --> DEC
    DEC --> ENG["Search engine Lunr Postgres Elasticsearch"]
    UI["SearchPage frontend"] -->|"query"| ENG

prompt: A company enables the GitHub auth provider. Users can log in, but the backend logs `Failed to sign-in, unable to resolve user identity` and the session never becomes valid. What is missing?
options: A sign-in resolver configured for the provider (for example `resolvers: - resolver: usernameMatchingUserEntityName`) that maps the GitHub profile to a User entity and issues a Backstage identity token
The `auth.environment` key, which must always equal `production`
A `kind: Location` entity pointing at GitHub's OAuth endpoint
The guest provider, which must be enabled alongside every other provider
optionNotes: Correct. Authentication proves who the user is at the provider; the sign-in resolver decides which Backstage identity (`user:default/<name>` plus ownership refs) they get. With no resolver, sign-in cannot complete. Built-in resolvers include `usernameMatchingUserEntityName` and `emailMatchingUserEntityProfileEmail`, and you can write custom ones with `signIn.resolvers`.
`auth.environment` selects which block under the provider (`development`, `production`) is used; it does not need to be `production` and its absence does not produce this error.
OAuth endpoints are not catalog entities; User and Group entities are what resolvers look up, typically ingested by an org entity provider.
Guest auth is an independent provider for unauthenticated access and is not required by other providers.
explanation: Backstage separates authentication (the provider verifying credentials) from sign-in (resolving a Backstage user identity and issuing a token). Each provider in `auth.providers` needs a `signIn.resolvers` list, either a built-in resolver or a custom one that returns `ctx.signInWithCatalogUser(...)` or `ctx.issueToken(...)`. If no resolver matches or none is configured, sign-in fails even though the OAuth flow succeeded.
example:
# app-config.yaml
auth:
  environment: development
  providers:
    github:
      development:
        clientId: ${AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
        clientSecret: ${AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
        signIn:
          resolvers:
            - resolver: usernameMatchingUserEntityName  # github login -> user:default/<login>

# backend
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-auth-backend'));
backend.add(import('@backstage/plugin-auth-backend-module-github-provider'));
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as "User"
    participant BE as "auth backend"
    participant GH as "GitHub OAuth"
    participant CAT as "Catalog"
    U->>BE: "start github login"
    BE->>GH: "OAuth flow"
    GH-->>BE: "profile login=alice"
    BE->>CAT: "resolver looks up user:default/alice"
    CAT-->>BE: "User entity + memberOf groups"
    BE-->>U: "Backstage identity token"

prompt: The `guest` auth provider is intended for local development; in production Backstage refuses to use it unless `dangerouslyAllowOutsideDevelopment: true` is explicitly set.
explanation: The guest provider (`@backstage/plugin-auth-backend-module-guest-provider`) signs everyone in as `user:development/guest` without credentials, which is convenient for `yarn start` but unsafe when the portal is reachable by others. Backstage therefore disables it outside `NODE_ENV=development` unless the operator sets `dangerouslyAllowOutsideDevelopment: true`, making the risk explicit.
example:
# app-config.yaml (development)
auth:
  providers:
    guest: {}   # everyone is user:development/guest

# app-config.production.yaml - normally omit guest entirely; if you must:
auth:
  providers:
    guest:
      dangerouslyAllowOutsideDevelopment: true
      userEntityRef: user:default/guest

prompt: A permission policy should let users delete catalog entities only when they own them. Which policy implementation achieves this correctly with the Backstage permissions framework?
options: For `catalog.entity.delete`, return `createCatalogConditionalDecision(request.permission, catalogConditions.isEntityOwner({ claims: user.info.ownershipEntityRefs }))`; the catalog then evaluates the rule per entity
Return `AuthorizeResult.ALLOW` and rely on the frontend to hide the delete button for non-owners
Add `permission.rules: [isEntityOwner]` to `app-config.yaml` and no code is required
Return `AuthorizeResult.DENY` for everyone and grant exceptions via the `catalog.rules` config
optionNotes: Correct. Resource permissions support conditional decisions: the policy returns a condition built from a permission rule (`isEntityOwner`) and the owning plugin applies it to the specific resource, so ownership is checked server-side per entity.
The framework is enforced in the backend; an unconditional ALLOW would let anyone delete via the API regardless of what the UI shows.
Policies are TypeScript classes implementing `PermissionPolicy`, registered through a backend module; there is no config-only rule binding.
`catalog.rules` controls which entity kinds may be ingested from locations, not who may delete them, and a blanket DENY would block owners too.
explanation: A `PermissionPolicy.handle(request, user)` returns `ALLOW`, `DENY`, or a `CONDITIONAL` decision. For resource-scoped permissions like `catalog.entity.delete`, conditional decisions reference permission rules (`isEntityOwner`, `hasAnnotation`, `isEntityKind`, and so on) that the resource-owning plugin evaluates against the actual entity. This keeps authorization on the server while allowing fine-grained per-resource logic; the policy is wired with `policyExtensionPoint.setPolicy` in a `createBackendModule` for `permission`.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    FE["Delete button"] -->|"authorize catalog.entity.delete"| PB["permission backend"]
    PB --> POL["PermissionPolicy.handle"]
    POL -->|"CONDITIONAL isEntityOwner"| PB
    PB -->|"condition"| CAT["catalog backend"]
    CAT -->|"evaluate rule on entity"| RES["ALLOW or DENY"]

prompt: Which annotation key does the Backstage Kubernetes plugin use by default to find the workloads belonging to an entity (matched against the `backstage.io/kubernetes-id` label on the cluster resources)?
explanation: The Kubernetes plugin looks up `backstage.io/kubernetes-id` on the entity and searches the configured clusters for objects carrying a label with the same key and value. Alternatives include `backstage.io/kubernetes-label-selector` for arbitrary selectors and `backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace` to limit the namespace. Clusters are declared under `kubernetes.clusterLocatorMethods` in `app-config.yaml`.
example:
# catalog-info.yaml
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  annotations:
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: payments-api
    backstage.io/kubernetes-namespace: payments

# deployment.yaml on the cluster
metadata:
  labels:
    backstage.io/kubernetes-id: payments-api   # must match the annotation value
diagram:
flowchart LR
    E["Entity annotation kubernetes-id payments-api"] --> KB["Kubernetes backend plugin"]
    KB -->|"clusterLocatorMethods"| C1["Cluster prod"]
    KB --> C2["Cluster staging"]
    C1 -->|"label kubernetes-id = payments-api"| W["Deployments Pods Services"]
    W --> TAB["Kubernetes tab on entity"]

prompt: A team is moving their Backstage instance from a laptop to a production Docker deployment. Which statements about the production configuration are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
options: Set `backend.database.client: pg` because the default `better-sqlite3` database is in-memory or file-based and unsuitable for production
Values like `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` in `app-config.yaml` are substituted from environment variables at startup
`app-config.production.yaml` is merged on top of `app-config.yaml` when the backend is started with `--config app-config.yaml --config app-config.production.yaml`
The Docker image must run `yarn start` for both frontend and backend as separate processes
`backend.baseUrl` and `app.baseUrl` can be left as `localhost` because the container's own hostname is used automatically
optionNotes: Correct. Production should use PostgreSQL (`client: pg` with `connection` host/port/user/password); SQLite loses data on restart unless a file path is set and does not scale.
Correct. The config loader replaces `${VAR}` with the environment variable value (and supports `$include` and `$file` for pulling in files and secrets).
Correct. Multiple `--config` flags are merged in order, later files overriding earlier keys, so the production file only needs the differences.

In the standard image (`packages/backend/Dockerfile`) the backend serves the built frontend bundle via the `app-backend` plugin, started with `node packages/backend --config ...`; `yarn start` is the dev workflow only.
Both `app.baseUrl` and `backend.baseUrl` must be set to the public URL users reach; CORS and OAuth callbacks depend on them, and nothing infers them automatically.
explanation: Production Backstage builds a single Docker image whose backend serves the frontend bundle and the APIs. You run it with `node packages/backend --config app-config.yaml --config app-config.production.yaml`, configuration files merge left to right, `${ENV_VAR}` placeholders are substituted at load time, PostgreSQL replaces SQLite, and `app.baseUrl`/`backend.baseUrl` must reflect the external hostname.
example:
# app-config.production.yaml
app:
  baseUrl: https://backstage.acme.com
backend:
  baseUrl: https://backstage.acme.com
  listen: ':7007'
  database:
    client: pg
    connection:
      host: ${POSTGRES_HOST}
      port: ${POSTGRES_PORT}
      user: ${POSTGRES_USER}

prompt: In a Backstage monorepo, which command launches the interactive generator that scaffolds a new frontend plugin, backend plugin, or backend module into the `plugins/` directory?
options: `yarn new`
`yarn dev`
`yarn backstage-cli repo build`
`npx @backstage/create-app`
optionNotes: Correct. `yarn new` (an alias for `backstage-cli new`) prompts for a package type such as `plugin`, `backend-plugin`, `backend-module`, or `web-library` and generates the package with a default structure, README, and dev setup.
`yarn dev` (or `yarn start`) runs the app and backend in development mode with hot reload; it does not create packages.
`backstage-cli repo build` compiles all packages in the repository for production; it is a build command, not a generator.
`create-app` bootstraps an entirely new Backstage app repository; you run it once, not per plugin.
explanation: The Backstage CLI (`@backstage/cli`) is exposed through package scripts: `yarn new` generates plugins and libraries, `yarn dev`/`yarn start` runs the app locally, `yarn tsc` type-checks, and `yarn build:backend` or `backstage-cli repo build` produces production bundles. Newly generated plugins land under `plugins/<id>` and are wired in with `backend.add(...)` or the frontend `App.tsx` routes.
example:
yarn new            # choose: plugin | backend-plugin | backend-module | ...
# ? Enter the ID of the plugin: todo
# creates plugins/todo (frontend) or plugins/todo-backend
yarn dev            # run frontend + backend with hot reload
yarn tsc && yarn build:backend   # type-check and build for production
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CLI["backstage-cli"] --> NEW["yarn new generate package"]
    CLI --> DEV["yarn dev run locally"]
    CLI --> BUILD["repo build production bundle"]
    NEW --> FP["plugins/todo frontend"]
    NEW --> BP["plugins/todo-backend"]
    BP -->|"backend.add"| APP["packages/backend"]
